Basal metabolic rate in the Red-crowned woodpecker (Melanerpes rubricapillus) was assessed through respirometry trials conducted under standardized thermal conditions. At a body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], the maximum resting oxygen consumption was measured at 96.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 96.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that aligns with expectations for a piciform of moderate body size. Newly hatched nestlings emerge at a remarkably modest mass, with the initial wet weight recorded at 4.5 grams [Ww0 = 4.5 grams], reflecting the altricial developmental mode typical of woodpeckers. This low birth mass necessitates an extended period of intensive parental provisioning and brooding before the chick can achieve endothermic independence.

Eggs incubated at a consistent temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C] require a developmental period of 10 days [ab = 10 days] before hatching occurs. This incubation duration is relatively brief compared to many other cavity-nesting birds of similar body size, potentially reflecting the species' preference for warm tropical lowland environments where elevated ambient temperatures reduce the energetic cost of maintaining optimal egg temperatures. The short incubation phase likely accelerates the overall nesting cycle, allowing the species to fit multiple breeding attempts into a single season while avoiding the peak of nest predation pressure. Following hatching, the altricial nestling enters a phase of rapid somatic growth sustained by the frequent delivery of arthropod prey by both parents.

Under the thermal regime typical of active metabolic periods in this species (41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]), several key developmental milestones are achieved. The nestling period concludes with fledging, which occurs at 32 days after hatching [tx = 32 days after hatching], a duration consistent with the 31 to 33 day range reported for related Melanerpes species at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. Gonadal maturation, signaling the onset of reproductive capacity, is attained considerably later at 67.5 days after hatching [tp = 67.5 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This extended interval between fledging and physiological sexual maturity provides ample time for the young bird to refine its foraging skills, establish a territory, and accumulate sufficient body reserves to support future reproductive effort.

Females ultimately reach an adult body mass of 52.45 grams [Wwi = 52.45 grams], placing them near the upper end of the reported body mass range for the species, which spans from 40 to 65 grams. This ultimate wet weight is achieved through a prolonged period of skeletal and muscular development that continues well beyond the fledging stage. In terms of reproductive output, females lay between 3 and 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 3 and 4 eggs per clutch], and they typically produce approximately 1.5 clutches annually [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 clutches annually], a rate that reflects the constraints of a protracted breeding season in a seasonally variable environment.

Longevity records for this species, compiled from banding studies conducted at 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], indicate that the maximum lifespan is approximately 2993 days [am = approximately 2993 days], a respectable duration for a small to medium-sized cavity-nesting bird. The age at which females initiate their first breeding attempt is somewhat delayed relative to the onset of puberty, with first brood production occurring at 1.2 years since birth [tR = 1.2 years since birth] at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This delay likely stems from the necessity of securing a suitable nesting cavity, which may be a limiting resource in many habitats, as well as the time required to perfect the excavation skills essential for successful reproduction in subsequent years.
